steps.narration: Watch the flash. Thirteen point eight billion years ago, everything we can observe was packed into a space far smaller than an atom, and then it expanded. Nothing on this graph predates that instant. Now watch what grows from it. Matter fans outward as space itself stretches. On one small planet, life takes root and branches into a tree. And from a single twig of that tree, people stream down the road of history toward this moment, toward you. The camera is following time around a clock, and every branch it passes is a chain of causes. Follow any of them backward and you arrive at the same flash. There is no other beginning to be found. Everything you will see from here is what that one moment made possible.

What you have just watched grow is a causality graph: a map of cause and effect. The idea behind it is simple and bold. Understand what caused what, and you can build a working model of the universe, from the Big Bang to this very moment. The model has three levels, and each stands on the one beneath it. Red is matter, the physical universe, obeying the Standard Model of particle physics and the laws of special and general relativity. Green is life, ordered by the tree of life and by the food chain. Blue is humanity: tribes, and the social market hierarchies they build. Time spirals through all three. We will read it level by level, link by link, until the chain arrives at you.

Begin with the question at the end of the line. Why are you here, right now? This path is one unbroken chain of causes. It starts at the Big Bang and ends at this exact moment, with you watching. Cause and effect runs one way only. Each link made the next one possible, and nothing that happened can be undone. We will follow that chain link by link, and at every stop the question stays the same. Each answer is a piece of the one that ends with you.

No ordinary ruler can hold thirteen point eight billion years, so here time runs clockwise on a spiral: a clock of deep time, stretched so that the first instants do not swallow everything after them. The Big Bang sits at six o'clock. Life appears near ten. At three o'clock, five thousand years ago, the clock lets go, and human history leaves the circle on a straight road, one steady step per year, all the way to now. The clock compresses eons. The road gives every year its due. Deep time is a circle, and history is a line.

Color means exactly one thing here. Red is matter. Green is life. Blue is humans. They are stacked in that order too, matter at the bottom, life above it, humans on top, because each level grew out of the one beneath. Life is assembled from matter, and people live on the energy that life captures. The order is not a ranking of importance. It is an order of dependence, and dependence is the shape of cause and effect. Remove a lower level, and everything above it falls.

Look at the distance from the inner track. It measures relevance to us. The inner track is our own lineage: the universe, the Milky Way, the Sun, the Earth, the first cells, the animals, the apes, the civilizations. Everything that split off along the way, other galaxies, other planets, other species, other peoples, drifts outward and fades. They are real. They are part of the story. But they are not on the direct chain of causes that ends here, with you, and so the graph lets them go.

No single scale fits this story. A billion years and a single lifetime cannot share one ruler. So the graph can be rescaled. Focus on any period and that stretch of the spiral straightens into a timeline of its own, so an eon or a childhood can fill the screen. Nothing is thrown away; it is only stretched or compressed until you can read it. This is how we will travel: zooming in where the causes are dense, and out where they are sparse. Afterwards, the U key and the number keys will do the same for you.

Here the chain begins. Thirteen point eight billion years ago, all space, matter and energy began expanding from an extremely hot and dense state. In a split second, inflation likely stretched tiny quantum ripples into the seeds of every galaxy that would ever form. Consider that for a moment. The pattern of the cosmos was set before the first second had passed. Every atom in your body traces back to here, which is why the red layer runs beneath everything else on this graph. Nothing above it could exist without it.

As the young universe cooled, quarks bound into protons and neutrons. Then matter met antimatter and annihilated, almost completely. For every billion particles that vanished, about one extra particle of matter survived. You are made of those survivors. Everything you will ever touch is made of those survivors. In the first few minutes, some of them fused into helium, leaving the universe about three quarters hydrogen and one quarter helium by mass. That plain mixture, two elements and little else, is the raw material of every star that came after.

About three hundred and eighty thousand years in, the universe had cooled enough for electrons to join those nuclei and make the first atoms. Light broke free. We still see it today, stretched and faint, as the cosmic microwave background: the oldest light there is. Then came the Dark Ages, roughly a hundred million years with no stars at all. But darkness is not stillness. Gravity worked the whole time, quietly pulling gas and dark matter into denser and denser clumps, preparing the ground for the first fire.

Those clumps grew dense enough to ignite, and the first stars were born. Made only of hydrogen and helium, most were probably giants that burned fast and died young. Their fusion, and the explosions that ended them, forged and scattered the first carbon, oxygen and iron: the elements that planets would need, and much later, life. Consider the chain. A star dies, and its ashes become the raw material of the next generation. Cause and effect, at the scale of the cosmos, and you are standing at the far end of it.

Stars gathered into the first galaxies, and here the red layer begins to branch. Most ordinary matter stayed behind as thin gas between the galaxies. Other galaxies drift outward, away from our track, because they are not on our chain. Watch the red layer spread and thin as space keeps expanding, faster since dark energy took over. The universe grows emptier with every passing eon. But one of those galaxies, one among countless others, is about to become home.

That galaxy is ours, the Milky Way. From about thirteen point six billion years ago it grew by merging with smaller galaxies, and generation after generation its stars lived and died. Each death enriched the galaxy's gas with carbon, oxygen and iron. Those same elements would one day build the Sun, the Earth, and you. The iron in your blood was made inside stars that burned out before the Sun was born. This is the stretch of the graph where that inheritance was forged.

Four point six billion years ago, a cold cloud of gas and dust in the disk of the Milky Way, enriched by all those earlier stars, collapsed under its own gravity. Most of it fell inward to become the Sun. The rest flattened into a spinning disk, and in that disk the planets would grow. Notice how the story narrows. From the whole universe to one galaxy, from one galaxy to one cloud. The chain of causes is tightening, and it is tightening toward you.

The Sun ignited. Today it holds ninety-nine point eight six percent of all the mass in the solar system, and it has shone steadily for more than four and a half billion years. Nearly all life on Earth runs on its light, which is why, when we reach the green level, every food chain will begin with it. The leftover disk built Jupiter and the other planets. Watch them split off here onto their own outer tracks, worlds of our own family that never became our road.

In that disk, about four point five four billion years ago, colliding planetesimals built the Earth, at just the right distance from the Sun for liquid water. The young planet melted and separated, iron sinking into a core, rock floating into a mantle. Later, that churning iron core would power a magnetic field strong enough to shield the air and the oceans. Water, rock and a shield: three causes laid down here that life will need, billions of years before anything is alive to need them.

Soon after, in the leading theory, a body the size of Mars, called Theia, struck the young Earth, and the debris gathered into the Moon. One collision, and a long line of effects. The Moon's gravity steadies the tilt of the Earth, which keeps seasons and climate more stable. It raises the tides that shaped coastlines and early life. Look up at it tonight and you are looking at the scar of an accident that has been steadying your world ever since.

Zircon crystals hint that Earth had liquid water by four point four billion years ago. And here, near ten o'clock, the green layer begins. Carbon traces in rocks from Greenland suggest microbes were living by three point seven billion years ago. Every living thing, from bacteria to you, descends from one common ancestor, and we all still share its genetic code. Life is the second level, and it is built entirely from the matter beneath it: ordinary atoms, forged in stars, arranged so that they copy themselves.

From that ancestor grows the green layer, the tree of life, ending in about sixteen hundred living groups, mostly families. It is ordered two ways at once. Along time, it follows descent: who came from whom. Within each branch, it follows the food chain, with the top predators toward the inside. That second order matters, because higher organisms live on the calories of the organisms beneath them. Our own lineage runs along the inside track, and every branch that split away bends outward and fades.

Early microbes lived on chemical energy, or on a simpler photosynthesis that made no oxygen. Then, probably by three billion years ago, cyanobacteria learned to split water using sunlight. Water and light were almost everywhere, so life's energy supply soared. This is the floor of every food chain: the place where sunlight first becomes calories. Everything above it, every grazer and every hunter, is living on borrowed starlight. And the waste product of that trick, oxygen, would go on to remake the whole planet.

About two point four billion years ago, that oxygen finally built up in the air. It poisoned many microbes and likely set off a long ice age. But it also let an ozone shield form, and it made energy-hungry life possible. Look closely at what happened here. Life changed the matter of the planet, and the changed planet changed life in return. The arrow of time still points one way, but between the levels of this graph, causes cross in both directions.

Oxygen made breathing a powerful new way to get energy. By about one point six five billion years ago, an archaeon had likely taken in an oxygen-breathing bacterium and, instead of digesting it, kept it. That bacterium became the mitochondrion, the power plant inside nearly every one of your cells. The extra energy let these complex cells grow large, and that was the step toward plants, fungi, animals and, in time, brains. A partnership between two microbes, and the thought you are having now depends on it.

With energy to spare, cells began to cooperate as bodies. A red alga called Bangiomorpha, about a billion years old, is the first known organism to reproduce sexually. Complex cells then branched into green plants, fungi and animals. And here the tree reveals something that appearance hides: fungi are closer kin to us than they are to plants. Read by descent rather than by looks, the tree of life keeps turning up relatives we never suspected.

After Snowball Earth, when ice reached all the way to the tropics, the thaws flooded the seas with nutrients. Soft-bodied Ediacaran creatures appeared, and then, from about five hundred and thirty-nine million years ago, most animal body plans arose within some twenty million years. Eyes, shells and predators set off an arms race. Once some animals ate others, the food chain grew new levels, and the pressure of hunting and being hunted shaped every animal that came after, including the one watching this.

Those Cambrian seas held our own branch, the chordates: small swimmers with a stiff rod along the back. Pressed by the arms race, their descendants grew a skull around a larger brain, and a backbone. Then came hinged jaws, which made them active predators and moved them up the food chain. That body plan became the blueprint for fish, for dinosaurs, and for you. Run a hand down your spine and you are touching an answer the Cambrian found.

Meanwhile, about four hundred and seventy million years ago, plants crept onto land. As they spread they turned bare rock into soil and drew carbon dioxide out of the air, and within about eighty-five million years the first forests stood. The continents were now livable for animals. On land as in the sea, the plants became the floor of the food chain, the calories that every land animal, and every land animal's hunter, would eventually live on.

Following the plants onto land came the lobe-finned fish. Their sturdy fin bones became our arm and leg bones, and about three hundred and seventy million years ago they gave rise to the tetrapods, animals with four limbs. They came through the Late Devonian extinction and carried the vertebrate body out of the water. Look at your own hands. The bones inside them trace back to a fin, and the fin to this branch of the tree.

Amphibians still had to return to the water to breed. Amniotes solved that with an egg that carries its own water, and the dry land was theirs. Then their lineage split in two. One side led to reptiles and birds. The other, our inner track, led to the mammals. Every split like this is a fork in the chain of causes. At each fork, only one path leads to you, and nothing at the time could have told which.

About two hundred and fifty-two million years ago, on the supercontinent Pangaea, vast eruptions in Siberia heated and acidified the planet. The Great Dying killed more than eighty percent of marine species, the worst extinction known. Here the red layer reached up and reset the green. Matter does not care what lives on it. Yet in the recovering world, two groups arose that matter enormously to this story: the dinosaurs, and the mammals.

Dinosaurs appeared about two hundred and thirty-three million years ago, and after the end-Triassic extinction they ruled the land for some one hundred and thirty-five million years. They held the top of the food chain. Beneath them, the first mammals were small nocturnal insect eaters, living in the shadows. Warm blood, fur and keen hearing kept them alive. For more than a hundred million years they waited, not knowing they were waiting, for a cause that had not yet arrived.

Then, sixty-six million years ago, an asteroid about ten kilometres wide struck what is now the Yucatan in Mexico. The impact winter killed about three quarters of all species, including every dinosaur except the birds. Watch the red layer strike the green. A rock from space, on one particular day, and the whole future of life turned. Without this impact, mammals, and we, might never have had our turn. Few causes on this graph are so clear, or so arbitrary.

With the dinosaurs gone, placental mammals spread into the empty niches: whales, bats, horses, cats, dogs and primates. Now notice the food chain order inside each branch. Hunters, like the cats, sit toward the inside. The plant eaters they prey on sit farther out. That is the logic of the whole green layer in miniature. Each level of the chain lives on the calories of the level beneath it, and the hunters at the top are always the few.

Here is why the green level is ordered the way it is. Plants capture sunlight and turn it into calories. Every step up the food chain eats the step beneath it, but passes on only roughly ten percent of the energy; the rest is spent as heat and work. Grasses feed moths, moths feed swallows, swallows feed falcons, and each arc is ten times thinner than the last. Higher organisms live on the organisms beneath them, so the top is always small. The same rule held in the Devonian seas and in the age of dinosaurs. Hold on to it. It will return, in money, when we reach the economy.

One small branch took to the trees. Primates gained grasping hands and forward-facing eyes. Many added keen color vision and large social groups, and living in those groups rewarded social intelligence, the ability to read and manage others. The apes went further still, with bigger brains and long childhoods for learning. Keep that idea of the social group in mind. The blue level of this graph grows from it.

As cooling climates opened African forests into woodland and grassland, our lineage split from the chimpanzees' by about seven million years ago. Walking upright freed the hands for carrying, and eventually for making tools. A small change in posture, with enormous consequences. Notice also where the cause came from: a shift in the climate, in the red layer, reshaped the green one. The planet changed, and one ape changed with it.

Free hands made the oldest known stone tools, three point three million years old. Tools opened up meat and marrow, richer calories that could fuel larger brains. Homo erectus spread out of Africa. Cooking with fire released still more energy from food, and swinging ice age climates rewarded adaptable minds. See the pattern. More energy, bigger brains, better ways to get more energy. It is a loop, and it will eventually lift one species clean off the green level.

About three hundred thousand years ago, our own species appears in Africa. With language and shared culture, knowledge could now build up faster than genes could change. This is a new kind of evolution, passed on by teaching rather than by inheritance alone, and it is the reason a third level, the blue one, is about to rise above the green. Of all the branches on the tree of life, only this one makes that climb.

Carrying that culture, modern humans spread out of Africa, starting around seventy thousand years ago, into Asia, Europe, Australia, and later the Americas. Along the way they mixed with Neanderthals and Denisovans, who later vanished. Every culture outside Africa descends from these migrations. Picture them: small bands walking into an empty world. These scattered bands are the first tribes, and the tribes are the beginning of the blue level.

When the last ice age ended, eleven thousand seven hundred years ago, the stable climate of the Holocene made farming possible. People domesticated grasses such as wheat and rice, whose large seeds store food, and began herding animals. A surplus of food meant that not everyone had to find food. That led to villages, then cities, writing and the first civilizations, and with them the first true hierarchies of people: the social orders that the blue level is drawn to show.

Farming turned wild families into servants. Wheat, sheep, goats and cattle left the green tree of life about ten thousand five hundred years ago and rose into a new layer just beneath the people: livestock and crops. It is the food chain again, but now one species is deliberately arranging the level beneath it as its own calorie supply. Today livestock outweighs all wild mammals by more than ten to one. The animal life of a planet, reshaped around one ape's appetite.

Beneath the farms lies the matter we dig up. Copper smelting, then bronze and iron, drew metal out of Earth's red layer. Later, coal, oil and concrete turned that trickle into about a hundred billion tonnes a year. So the stack repeats itself inside the human world. People on top, the life we farm below, the matter we extract below that. The same three levels, in the same order, now under the hand of a single species.

In the blue level, each civilization is drawn as a stream, and its width is its relative power. Those widths come from the Histomap, a chart drawn by Sparks in nineteen thirty-one, and for the last century from each country's share of world economic output. When the Histomap begins, about four thousand years ago, Egyptian, Mesopotamian, Anatolian, Indian and Chinese peoples are already flowing side by side, west to east. From here on, each people has a lifespan: a rise, a width, and a fall.

Look inside one of those streams and you find a population curve split by sex, men on one side and women on the other. Each thin line is a single lifespan, rising and falling with a modeled social market value, and each line stands for a number of people shown on screen. Famous people glow, like Hatshepsut and Hammurabi. This is the social market hierarchy of a people, drawn as a shape. Thousands of years of lives, and you can see them all at once.

Why are so many of these lines short? In the ancient world, life expectancy at birth was only about twenty-six years, mostly because so many children died. Adults who reached fifteen often lived into their forties, fifties, or sixties. Compare the two halves as well. Women's small edge in lifespan grew as childbirth became safer, to about five years today. Every short line here is a chain of causes cut off early, and every long one is a chain that held.

Streams collide, and streams split. Egypt and the Hittites fought to a draw at Kadesh, then signed one of the oldest known peace treaties. Yet around three thousand two hundred years ago, the Late Bronze Age collapse brought down the Hittites and the palaces of the Aegean. In time, from that wreckage, the Greek city-states grew. Collapse is not the end of a chain. Often it is the beginning of the next, and no one living through it can see what it will build.

As Iron Age states grew larger and richer, thinkers across Eurasia began asking how to live well: Confucius and Laozi in China, the Buddha in India, Socrates in Greece. Their ideas have outlived every empire on this map, and they still guide billions of people. Consider what that means. In the blue level, some of the strongest causes are not armies or harvests. They are thoughts, carried from mind to mind across a hundred generations.

Cyrus the Great built Persia into the largest empire the world had yet seen. Alexander the Great conquered it in under a decade. But when he died at thirty-two, his empire split among his generals. Watch Greek rule flow into Ptolemaic Egypt and the Seleucid Empire, carrying Greek culture all the way from Egypt to India. Power can rise within a single lifetime, and split the moment that lifetime ends.

Rome absorbed Greek culture, destroyed its rival Carthage in the Punic Wars, and, after Julius Caesar's civil war, became an empire under Augustus. It united the Mediterranean with roads, law and the Latin language. Its eastern half, Byzantium, kept Greek learning alive until fourteen fifty-three. Watch how wide the Roman stream grows. That width is relative power, and the roads and laws behind it are causes the world still lives with.

The scriptures of little Israel and Judah shaped two great faiths. Christianity spread along Rome's roads after Jesus and Paul, and Islam united Arabia under Muhammad. Arab caliphates then stretched from Spain to India, preserving Greek science and carrying Indian numerals west, the numerals most of the world writes with today. Empires are wide streams that end. Faiths and ideas are threads that pass through them and keep going.

Steppe nomads such as the Huns pushed Germanic peoples into a weakened Rome, and by four hundred and seventy-six the Western Empire had fallen. Watch one stream split into many. The Franks, whose realm peaked under Charlemagne, and the other Germanic kingdoms became the roots of France, Germany, England and much of Europe. One civilization's end is the beginning of many others. On this graph, a fall is a branching.

In the twelve hundreds, Genghis Khan and his heirs built the largest contiguous land empire in history. By linking Eurasia, it carried trade and ideas, and also the Black Death. As it fractured, new powers grew from its edges, among them Muscovy, later Russia, and the Ottoman Turks. One empire's rise and fall set the shape of the map for centuries, and the shape of the map set the lives of everyone born into it.

Around fourteen fifty, Gutenberg's printing press made books cheap, and printed ideas spread faster than any ruler could stop them. That fueled Luther's Reformation and the science of Galileo and Newton. Meanwhile, Columbus's voyage in fourteen ninety-two linked Europe and the Americas, reshaping trade, crops and peoples on both sides of the ocean. Information itself had become a cause, moving faster than armies, and the world would never again be as slow.

Printing, science and trade fed two revolutions in the late seventeen hundreds. Britain's American colonies declared independence in seventeen seventy-six, while James Watt's steam engines helped launch Britain's Industrial Revolution. Machines multiplied what each worker could make. Watch the British stream swell with power, and then the American. Coal and steam were drawing energy out of the red layer on a scale no people had ever commanded, and the blue level began to grow as nothing in it had grown before.

Industry paid for science, and science lengthened lives. Germ theory, vaccines, antibiotics and high-yield crops cut child deaths and more than doubled life expectancy since eighteen hundred, to over seventy years today. So the lifelines here grow long, and the world's population balloons past eight billion. More people, living longer, is one of the largest effects on the whole graph, and it rests on every level beneath it: the sunlight, the soil, the ore and the oil.

The same industry made war industrial. World War One killed about twenty million people, and World War Two about seventy-five million. In this model, roughly a quarter of German and a fifth of Soviet men of military age die. You can see that scar as a gap on the men's side of those streams. Behind each missing line is a family, and a chain of causes that ended early. Look at the gap. It is the shape of a generation that did not come home.

By nineteen forty-five, the United States was by far the widest stream, now measured by share of world economic output. Afterwards, Japan and Germany rebuilt into economic giants. Since Deng Xiaoping's reforms began in nineteen seventy-eight, China has grown into the largest economy by purchasing power, and India is rising fast. Relative power never sits still. Watch the widths shift between west and east, and remember that each width is millions of lives.

For most of history the human branch was a thin thread. After eighteen hundred, coal, medicine and fertilizer let the population leap from one billion to eight billion, and every layer beneath us exploded with it: livestock, cropland, fuels, ores and sand. This is what it looks like when the top of the stack grows. Every level underneath must carry the weight, and the planet is now visibly shaped by the species at its top.

Every famous life is a glowing line inside its civilization, and threads show who shaped whom: Newton to Einstein, teacher to student. Ideas are causes too, passed from one mind to the next across centuries. Press F to see everyone alive at whatever moment you are looking at, and follow any of them from birth to death. It is the same chain of cause and effect we have followed since the Big Bang, now at the scale of a single life.

Now zoom into one stream: the United States, from nineteen fifty to today. Here the population is simulated in detail, built from United Nations age pyramids and from American marriage and divorce rates, with men on one side and women on the other. Hundreds of millions of lives, drawn as one shape. This stream is also a doorway. At its end, the graph opens into the second part of the model, the economy.

Each line follows one life from birth to death. From age eighteen its height follows a modeled social market value. In this model, women's value peaks young, men's rises with wealth into middle age, and having children lowers both. Be clear about what this is. It is a model of a popular idea, drawn so that it can be examined and argued with. It is not a measurement of anyone's worth. A line's height tells you what the model assumes, not what a person is.

No screen could draw hundreds of millions of Americans, so each line stands for a number of people. Watch that count on the screen change as you zoom in and out. Lines with higher value run nearest the center line between the two halves, and married couples are drawn in toward it, side by side. Position on this graph always means something. Here it means value and partnership, and the count tells you how many lives each line carries.

When World War Two ended, returning soldiers, early marriages and prosperity produced the baby boom. American births surged from nineteen forty-six to nineteen sixty-four. Children's lines start from their parents' lines, so you can watch the boomers branch out of the Greatest and Silent generations. This is cause and effect at its most personal: a family making the next family, and a war's end written into the shape of a population.

From nineteen sixty to nineteen eighty, the divorce rate in the United States more than doubled, and later the marriage rate fell by more than a third. Watch more paired lines come apart, often after children have branched from them. Millennials, Generation Z and Generation Alpha inherit a world of later marriages and fewer children. That inheritance, too, is a cause, and whatever comes next will be shaped by it.

The human branch runs straight to its tip. The last century is a thin slice of it, the last year a hairline, the last second invisible. Yet every blue line is still arriving here. Matter and life faded out before the branch began, but only on the screen. Everything they made possible continues in us: in your body, in the food you eat, in the ground beneath you. Thirteen point eight billion years, and all of it is still present in this one second.

At the glowing Now beacon, all three levels arrive together. The hydrogen in your body dates from the Big Bang. Your carbon and oxygen were made in stars. Three point seven billion years of life, and every empire, war and family in blue, shaped the world you were born into. Every line on this graph either ended somewhere along the way, or led here, to you. You are not watching the story. You are what the story has made so far.

Step back. From the Big Bang at six o'clock, around the clock of deep time, and down the road of human history, every cause on this graph led to this moment. Matter, held together by the laws of physics. Life, built on matter, each creature living on the ones beneath it. People, built on life, organized into tribes and hierarchies that rise and fall. Understand that chain and you hold a working model of the universe. This moment is not the end of the chain. It is where the next one begins, and you are a link in it. Explore any era and follow the lines from cause to effect. The newest link, the one people build on one another, is an economy. We go there next.
